paragraphs.source_en: Excavations in both the Acacus and the Tassili have shown similarities in the settlement pattern. In all the excavated shelters which are situated in large wadies, Pleistocene occupation, attributed probably to the Aterian culture (Cremaschi et al. 1998), was separated from the Early Holocene occupation by a layer of aeolian sand, indicating an arid climate. Uan Afuda in the Acacus provides the oldest dates for human occupation. The Aterian dated to 90,000–69,000 (Garcea 1998) was followed by the successive layer dated to 9,765+105 BP (calBP 11,096+179). At Tin Hanakaten in the Tassili, the undated Aterian industry was separated by sand from a successive layer dated to 9,420+200 BP (calBP 10,726±300)(Aumassip 1980-1).

paragraphs.source_en: The Holocene occupation in all the shelters starts in the 10th millennium BP which correlates with the climatic record indicating a wet phase across the Sahara (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996a).

paragraphs.source_en: In the Acacus and in the neighbouring mountains water has been abundant since the 16th millennium BP. It is unlikely that in a humid environment life would be completely absent. However, why is there no evidence of human presence before the 10th millennium BP? There is actually no archaeological evidence for human occupation inside the shelters but the surface outside the shelters contains large quantities of lithic tools of various dates and diagnostic style, from rough flakes to tiny microlithics. These are objects without stratigraphical context and are therefore difficult to date. Di Lernia (1999) postulates that the Epipalaeolithic period actually started before the first dates in the Acacus shelters, as he found open-air sites with a lithic industry characterised by blades evolving towards the Epipalaeolithic lithic style.

paragraphs.source_en: Before the 10th millennium BP small groups of hunter-gatherers may have lived out in the open. This is supported by the fact that the Aterian culture of the Pleistocene period is mainly attested in the open and only rarely in shelters (Hachid 1998; Aumassip 2004). The Aterian people preferred to live outside shelters, near water courses or water bodies, and this pattern of settlement may have continued until the 10th millennium BP.
